speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, last night I was cut off in the full flood of my remarks because time ran out on me. I do not know whether you were in the chair at that time, but I am sure, had you been, that you must have been disappointed, because I was about to deal with the speech made last Wednesday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Of course, in the opinion of that minister there is nothing more important than a speech which he makes. I wish to pay my tribute to the exalted position he occupies. As I said, his speech dealt with the subject of external affairs. Unless we are very clear on that subject our defence policy will not make sense. Our understanding all along has been that foreign policy is declared and that our defence policy then is designed to meet that foreign policy, or is tailored to fit it.
Last Wednesday I was hoping that the Secretary of State for External Affairs would give us a very clear statement with regard to Canada's position concerning our external relations, and where we stand in the field of foreign affairs. The minister thought he had done that; but when one reads his speech he finds that there are some question marks. In the course of the speech the minister dealt with the subject of the proposed reorganization of our defence forces. He gave us no evidence in this regard, but he did give us what he considered to be a weighty opinion. After all, the speech that was given to us was that of none other than the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Normally one bows when his name is mentioned. He may have thought he was speaking to his friends in the ambassadorial circles around town instead of to those persons who know him well in this House of Commons.
I was not as interested as some persons might have been by this apparently weighty
April 12. 1987	COMMONS
opinion expressed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He did not tell us that he had examined the evidence of the committee. Heretofore he has not exhibited any great interest in defence matters; yet apparently he felt competent to tell us what should be done.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs attempted to clear up the situation with regard to our alliances, yet he left a great escape route-a loophole. I should like to read these words of the minister which appear at page 14565 of Hansard:
I do not exclude the possibility that in the future it may become feasible, and indeed I hope it will, to withdraw our forces from Europe and to make our entire contribution from bases in Canada.
This is diplomatic language. Every word is very carefully selected, because it will be read and interpreted around the word. Here we have the Secretary of State for External Affairs hoping that we will be able to withdraw our forces from Europe and make our entire contribution from bases in Canada.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
At a meeting of the external affairs committee last spring I asked him whether it would be a feasible proposition to use our transport airplanes to rotate our troops in Europe more frequently, rather than leave them there for a year. I asked him whether or not it would be feasible to rotate the troops much more frequently, rather than at considerable expense leaving them over there with their dependants for a year. I suggested they could be rotated at intervals of perhaps three or six months. I do not remember his exact words but he indicated his assent to that proposition. He then received phone calls and communications from countries in Europe, and other countries with whom we are in alliance in this situation, and he became greatly disturbed because he thought I had trapped him into giving an answer. Actually I was just looking for information.
Periodically when I find that not enough attention is being paid to the minister for external affairs in the house I ask him a question on orders of the day. Frequently he does not answer my questions and we are deprived of information. Nevertheless I like to draw attention to him so his name gets in the papers, because I know he loves the publicity.
The minister has now enunciated his doctrine of withdrawing our forces from Europe and making our entire contribution from bases in Canada. He then went on to say this:
National Defence Act Amendment
But such a course of action is neither feasible nor desirable at this moment-
He had to have an escape hatch. What does he have in mind as to when this may take place?-next week, next month, later on this year or next year? The minister for external affairs failed in this regard to give the house the exact circumstances relating to our foreign policy. Why did he not make a statement which would not be subject to misinterpretation? He could have told us that we were going to maintain our forces in Europe under our alliances in NATO throughout 1967, 1968 and 1969 unless the NATO allies together in conference decided there should be a change. He did not do that. He left everything in mid-air. I suggest the statement indicates that there is nothing certain about the maintenance of our forces in Europe. In fact the minister hopes that they may be withdrawn.
Later on in the same paragraph he created another escape hatch which he would use if One queried him about this during orders of the day, when he said:
Until we can be sure that we can make an appropriate and effective military contribution entirely from Canada, or until a Canadian contribution is no longer considered necessary, we should continue contributing forces in Europe as part of a collective defence.
He says we should continue, but he does not say that we are actually going to continue. He leaves the Canadian public in a state of uncertainty as to whether or not we are really going to maintain our NATO alliance and our contributions in Europe, or at what strength. He said nothing about our responsibility in antisubmarine warfare. We have a commitment to NATO to maintain an effective and large antisubmarine force. We heard evidence before the committee on defence that the antisubmarine force no longer is as large as it was, and that ships now available are undermanned, with some of them tied up for want of personnel.
The minister said nothing about NORAD; yet the whole purpose of getting him into this debate was to obtain from him a clear and definitive statement on foreign affairs. I was very disappointed in the minister, as I am almost every week, because in the course of my remarks I complimented him and referred to his lengthy career in the house. I outlined the highlights of that career and the many good things he has accomplished. I did not mention any of his failures. I was very complimentary to him. But when he rose to speak he did not return the compliment, in fact he
April 12, 1967

(5:50 p.m.)
National Defence Act Amendment was inclined to ridicule me. I was rather hurt because I had tried to be friendly and help the minister, under whose direction Canada's prestige abroad has fallen to an all time low. I tried to help him, so his spirits would be revived. Not only did he brush me aside but he misinterpreted what I had said. Perhaps he did so unconsciously or inadvertently, but he did refer to what I had said about peace restoring as peacekeeping.
The expression peace restoring has been used on many occasions by the Minister of National Defence and others. There is a vast difference between peace keeping and peace restoring. Let me read what the minister of defence said on December 7, 1966 as reported at page 10832 of Hansard:
Even the success or failure of peace restoring or peace keeping operations can 'well depend on the speed with which decisions are reached and the force and its equipment delivered to the trouble zone.
The phrase peace restoring was used during the committee study of this bill. I had hoped that the minister for external affairs would tell us something about peace restoring. He did not do that, but rather referred to peacekeeping.
There are two distinct methods of operating, one is peace keeping, which we are doing at the present time in Cyprus and in the Gaza strip as well as other places where we have observers. Peace restoring involves sending a punitive expedition to a place where trouble has broken out. That force must be prepared to engage in warfare and put out the so-called brushfire or trouble that has occurred.
At page 10835 of Hansard for December 7 last year the minister is recorded as having said:
It can be said with assurance that Canada's influence in the years ahead and its capacity to act in favour and settlement of disputes that endanger peace will grow with its own development.
Note that the minister referred to the settlement in disputes. There is a dispute taking place now in Aden. People are firing rifles at each other and throwing bombs. Last week there was a dispute between Israel and Syria when aircraft were attacking each other. Our Canadian forces, in order to perform in that capacity-settling	disputes or restoring
peace-must be prepared to enter into warfare to enforce peace. Let us have a statement from the minister for external affairs in this regard. He did not give us such a statement, but dodged the issue. He is very skilful at dodging issues. So when I hoped that he would talk about peace restoring, he talked about peace keeping.

My proposal for peacekeeping was that it should be separate and apart from our armed forces. The Secretary of State for External Affairs had to admit that what we are carrying on in Cyprus and the Gaza strip is a police operation. We do not require heavy tanks, close support aeroplanes or artillery for that job. Those things are not there with our people; they have light arms for self-protection. That is the way in which we are performing in our missions abroad. It is a police operation. I was suggesting that we continue that type of operation, within the limits of reasonable expense and with the co-operation of others in the United Nations, but that we do it, not by using our navy, army and air force, the forces that are equipped for war, but by using a special, elite force which is a peace keeping force.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs rejected the idea and thought we should continue to do what we are now doing. The weakness of the minister's position is just this: At the external affairs committee yesterday-and I am not reporting the committee hearings; I am reporting what appeared in the newspapers and on television last night- the minister made a lengthy statement with regard to Viet Nam and outlined a fourpronged program to be put into effect immediately, if possible, when that war comes to an end. This was his contribution to the situation in Viet Nam and part of the continuing process of keeping in the limelight with regard to matters concerning peace. The minister periodically has a press conference, an exposure on television, or makes a speech somewhere, and if all those things fail he can call together the committee on external affairs and get his publicity that way. In the course of that exercise he suggested that if and when peace does come in Viet Nam, Canada is prepared to make a contribution with regard to the maintenance of that peace, which means another peace keeping force when the war comes to an end.
How many people would be involved in that peace keeping force? Speculation in the press is that we might require as many as 30,000 men for that purpose. I do not know whether that figure is inflated. But if Canada participates, it cannot be just on a small scale; it would surely have to be on a battalion scale, two battalions, or something like that. You might find that you were providing for activities in Viet Nam 1,000 people from our armed forces over and above the 800 that are in Cyprus, as well as the others that are
April 12, 1967	COMMONS
in the Gaza strip and elsewhere. We have about 2,000 people abroad right now on peace keeping missions.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has offered another group for another peace keeping mission. Where is he going to get the men? Our national defence figures indicate a serious depletion in the strength of our forces. They used to number about 120,000 or 125,000; now they are down to 104,000. All the 13 infantry battalions are, on the average, under strength and have been for some months. There is a deficiency of 4,000 infantrymen in those battalions. There is a deficiency of 4,000 men to man the ships in our antisubmarine role.
Where is the Secretary of State for External Affairs going to get these men?- Is he going to reduce our commitments to NATO? I submit that we are not meeting our commitments to NATO at this very moment, because we have reduced the effectiveness of our air division overseas. The two infantry brigades in Canada that are earmarked under NATO for an emergency are not up to strength. The antisubmarine force which is earmarked for NATO purposes is under strength. So where is the Secretary of State for External Affairs going to get another 600 or 1,000 men for a peace keeping operation in Viet Nam, if peace is declared in that country? This shows the extent of the confusion in the government ranks with regard to these matters.
If the minister is going to make an offer-he has publicly made the offer now, and if peace is declared this summer Canada would be obligated to do something about it-we would have to provide a force, if par-

liament consented, reduce our commitments to NATO, and reduce our commitments for home defence. So it is quite clear that we have not had given to us by the Secretary of State for External Affairs a clear exposition of our obligations in foreign affairs and to our allies.
Why did he not tell us last Wednesday, when he was making his speech, what his proposition was with regard to Viet Nam? He did not disclose It in the House of Commons, and exposed his hand at the committee hearings on Tuesday, and to the press and the Canadian public over television. So we now have another commitment just around the corner, and we are already short of men in the forces and are failing to meet our present commitments. That, sir, constitutes part of what I intended to say last night with regard to the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
